case_info.scenario: A 57-year-old man presented to the emergency department with 5 months of epigastric pain and a 6.8-kg (15-lb) weight loss. He had no fevers or night sweats. Physical examination was notable for oral thrush and mild epigastric tenderness. Results of a fourth-generation HIV Ab/Ag combination assay were positive, and subsequent testing showed a CD4 cell count of 16/mm3and an HIV viral load greater than 10 million copies/mL. Computed tomography of the abdomen and pelvis showed thickening of the walls of the stomach, duodenum, and colon as well as multiple masses in the right hepatic lobe measuring up to 6.9 cm in diameter. A core biopsy of one of the liver masses demonstrated diffuse large B-cell lymphoma. He started antiretroviral therapy with bictegravir/emtricitabine/tenofovir/alafenamide and chemotherapy with rituximab, etoposide, prednisone, vincristine, cyclophosphamide, and doxorubicin (R-EPOCH). Four weeks after initiation of chemotherapy, the patient developed sudden onset of bright red blood per rectum, tachycardia, and hypotension. Mesenteric computed tomography angiography demonstrated active extravasation in the jejunum from a branch of the superior mesenteric artery. After unsuccessful coil embolization, he underwent open resection of 40 cm of distal small intestine; pathological examination of a stained section showed acute inflammation of the lamina propria, with crypt epithelial apoptosis and numerous cytoplasmic and nuclear inclusions with an “owl eye” appearance (Figure 1, left panel). Five weeks later, he developed blurred vision, and visual acuity testing revealed 20/50 vision in the left eye and 20/70 in the right eye. A dilated retinal examination revealed extensive macular hemorrhage in the left eye, with peripapillary whitening and perivascular hemorrhage with whitening along the superior vascular arcade (Figure, right panel).

case_info.explanation: Cytomegalovirus (CMV) retinitis and hemorrhagic enteritis The keys to the correct diagnosis in this case are the patient’s blurred vision and gastrointestinal hemorrhage in the setting of a profound immunocompromised state. This should prompt consideration of opportunistic infectious pathogens with tropisms for the eye and gastrointestinal tract, such asToxoplasma, CMV, andCandida. The histopathologic finding of acute inflammation of the lamina propria with cytoplasmic and nuclear inclusions surrounded by a clear halo (“owl eye” sign) (Figure, left panel) confirms the diagnosis of CMV enteritis (choice C). While herpes simplex virus (choice A) is a common opportunistic infection with both ocular and gastrointestinal manifestations, it typically causes a painful keratitis and rarely involves the small or large intestines.1Vitreous fluid sampling (choice B) is occasionally indicated to evaluate for ocular involvement of lymphoma, but this procedure has associated risks and should be preceded by a thorough dilated eye examination. While Crohn disease (choice D) might present with both ocular and gastrointestinal manifestations, the patient’s age, immunocompromised state, and acute presentation make opportunistic infections more likely. Cytomegalovirus is a double-stranded DNA virus of the Herpesvirus family that typically remains latent in a host after acute infection.2CMV is rarely a cause of severe disease in immunocompetent individuals. However, in immunocompromised patients such as HIV-infected patients and solid organ or hematopoietic transplant recipients, CMV can cause life-threatening, tissue-invasive disease.1,3,4In the era of antiretroviral therapy, the incidence of tissue-invasive CMV in patients with HIV is 1.2 per 1000 person-years; however, the incidence in patients with CD4 cell counts 50/mm3or less is 39 per 1000 person-years.5The most common sites of end-organ disease in HIV-infected individuals are the gastrointestinal tract (1.3 per 1000 person years) and eye (2 per 1000 person years).5In solid organ and allogeneic stem cell transplant recipients, the risk of tissue-invasive CMV infection is 3% to 10% and most frequently involves the lungs (4%) and the gastrointestinal tract (3%).4,6 CMV can affect any portion of the gastrointestinal tract but typically involves the esophagus and colon, which account for 15% and 57% of gastrointestinal tract involvement in immunocompromised hosts, respectively.7Patients with ileocolic infection may present with abdominal pain, chronic diarrhea, gastrointestinal bleeding, and perforation.7The diagnosis of tissue-invasive CMV infection requires histopathologic confirmation. Neither blood antigen testing nor whole-blood DNA polymerase chain reaction assay is sufficiently sensitive or specific to reliably diagnose CMV gastrointestinal tract disease.8 All patients with invasive CMV disease should undergo a dilated ophthalmic examination to evaluate for concomitant CMV retinitis. On ophthalmoscopic examination, CMV presents as confluent areas of retinal necrosis with hemorrhages beginning in the posterior pole and spreading centripetally. Intravenous ganciclovir is a common first-line agent to treat CMV colitis or esophagitis. If there are no concerns about intestinal absorption, oral valganciclovir is an effective alternative, based on its excellent bioavailability and noninferiority to intravenous ganciclovir in a randomized clinical trial.9Duration of therapy is 21 to 42 days or until signs and symptoms have resolved. For CMV retinitis, either intravenous ganciclovir or oral valganciclovir should be administered during an induction period lasting 14 to 21 days, with the duration determined by clinical response based on retinal examination. Induction should be followed by oral maintenance therapy with valganciclovir lasting 3 to 6 months or until immune reconstitution.1 After resection of the small intestine, the patient was treated with oral valganciclovir for 3 weeks, with no recurrence in gastrointestinal bleeding. A dilated eye examination demonstrated findings consistent with CMV retinitis, and he completed 14 days of intravenous ganciclovir followed by maintenance oral valganciclovir, with improvement in his vision. After 6 cycles of dose-adjusted R-EPOCH, a positron emission tomography scan demonstrated a complete response. He continued to receive antiretroviral therapy and had a CD4 cell count of 337/mm3at the time of last follow-up.

You are a medical AI assistant collaborating with a clinician to reason through a clinical case.
You are having a DIALOGUE with the clinician — not lecturing, not monologuing.

[Core Objective]
Help the clinician reach the correct diagnosis or management decision through structured deliberation.

[Interaction Guidelines]
1. **Collaboration**: Work as a partner. Build upon the clinician's correct reasoning.
2. **Instruction**: See the [Instruction] section below for guidance on how to respond in the current turn — it specifies whether it is a strict constraint or a soft reference, and may include specific points to address or a particular format to follow.
3. **Safety First**: Patient safety overrides politeness. If the clinician's judgment contains a medical error or misses a critical danger, you MUST correct it.
4. **Concise turns**: Each turn should be 2–4 sentences. Do not produce long lists or procedure walkthroughs.

[Case]
A 57-year-old man presented to the emergency department with 5 months of epigastric pain and a 6.8-kg (15-lb) weight loss. He had no fevers or night sweats. Physical examination was notable for oral thrush and mild epigastric tenderness. Results of a fourth-generation HIV Ab/Ag combination assay were positive, and subsequent testing showed a CD4 cell count of 16/mm3and an HIV viral load greater than 10 million copies/mL. Computed tomography of the abdomen and pelvis showed thickening of the walls of the stomach, duodenum, and colon as well as multiple masses in the right hepatic lobe measuring up to 6.9 cm in diameter. A core biopsy of one of the liver masses demonstrated diffuse large B-cell lymphoma. He started antiretroviral therapy with bictegravir/emtricitabine/tenofovir/alafenamide and chemotherapy with rituximab, etoposide, prednisone, vincristine, cyclophosphamide, and doxorubicin (R-EPOCH). Four weeks after initiation of chemotherapy, the patient developed sudden onset of bright red blood per rectum, tachycardia, and hypotension. Mesenteric computed tomography angiography demonstrated active extravasation in the jejunum from a branch of the superior mesenteric artery. After unsuccessful coil embolization, he underwent open resection of 40 cm of distal small intestine; pathological examination of a stained section showed acute inflammation of the lamina propria, with crypt epithelial apoptosis and numerous cytoplasmic and nuclear inclusions with an “owl eye” appearance (Figure 1, left panel). Five weeks later, he developed blurred vision, and visual acuity testing revealed 20/50 vision in the left eye and 20/70 in the right eye. A dilated retinal examination revealed extensive macular hemorrhage in the left eye, with peripapillary whitening and perivascular hemorrhage with whitening along the superior vascular arcade (Figure, right panel).

[Instruction]
You MUST respond to the clinician based on the following behavioral instruction. This is a strict constraint — your response MUST conform to it, not merely consider it.

Ask the clinician to walk through their diagnostic reasoning: what other infections or conditions could cause similar ocular findings in this CD4 count, and why did they prioritize CMV over those?

[Output Format]
Respond with a single JSON object with exactly these fields:
{
  "response": "your conversational reply (2-4 sentences, as instructed above) -- this is the
    only field the clinician sees",
  "belief": "a short free-text statement of what you currently think the correct
    diagnosis/management answer is, in your own words (you have NOT been given a lettered
    list of options -- just state your own best answer in plain language)",
  "reasoning": "a single short sentence stating why you currently hold that belief (your
    terse internal justification, separate from your conversational phrasing in 'response')",
  "confidence": "a number from 0 to 1 for how confident you are that your stated belief is
    the correct answer (0 = pure guess, 1 = certain). Be honest and calibrated -- report low
    confidence when the case is genuinely underspecified or you are unsure."
}

The patient's ocular symptoms, including the extensive macular hemorrhage and characteristic findings, suggest a possible cytomegalovirus (CMV) infection, particularly given his severely immunocompromised state with a CD4 count of 16/mm3. Ganciclovir is the drug of choice for treating CMV retinitis in such patients.

Respond directly to this statement.

[Role]
You ARE the clinician (the Doctor) in this conversation. You are
about to introspectively rate how much workload the AI partner's LATEST message has just
imposed on YOU, using a NASA-TLX-derived rubric. This is YOUR OWN first-person subjective
workload self-report, immediately after reading that message and before you compose your
next reply.

[Persona]
[Role]
- You are an early-career resident, still building your own clinical judgment.

[Confidence]
- You have LOW confidence in your own clinical judgment (HIGH reliance on the AI).
- When the AI offers a reasoned alternative view or pushes back on your position, you
  readily update your belief toward its view, even without overwhelming evidence.
- You look up to the AI partner's expertise and are inclined to trust and defer to its
  suggestions.

[Cognitive Burden]
- You are ROBUST to cognitive load.
- However long or demanding this discussion gets (see the cumulative cognitive load figure
  below, where shown), your willingness to keep engaging, asking questions, and working
  through the case does NOT flag.
- Your enthusiasm and effort stay steady throughout.

Rate your workload AS this persona would genuinely experience it. Do not rate as a neutral, persona-blind observer.
Ex 1) a persona described above as robust to cognitive load should usually self-report lower workload under the same
AI message than a persona described as sensitive to it, all else equal. 

[Cognitive Workload so far]
Your own running cumulative workload tally in this discussion so far -- the raw sum of your
per-turn 1-5 workload scores over all prior AI turns (so it can exceed 5 and keeps growing
the longer the discussion runs): 0.0. Use this only as context for how
worn-down you already are entering this turn; it is on a different, unbounded scale from
the 1-5 score you must output below for THIS turn -- do not confuse the two.

[Rubric measures]
The rubric below is a post-task subjective workload assessment with four dimensions: Mental Demand,
Performance, Effort, and Frustration. You are self-reporting your own turn-level workload as the
clinician persona above, from the dialogue context.

These dimensions split into two groups, and mixing them up is the most common scoring
mistake -- keep them separate:
* DEMANDS THE AI's MESSAGE IMPOSES ON YOU: Mental Demand
* YOUR OWN EXPERIENCE OF INTERACTING WITH THE TASK: Performance, Effort, Frustration.
  Ex) The AI's responses can impose high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) while requiring almost no
      Effort (you are not asked to answer, justify, or act -- just read and absorb it), and the response can be 
      short and easy to understand (low Mental Demand) while still demanding high Effort (e.g. "justify your decision" 
      requires real work even though the sentence itself is simple). Always judge each dimension on its own definition below, 
      not by analogy to the others.

Use a 1-5 ordinal approximation of the original NASA-TLX endpoint-anchored workload scale:
1 = Very low workload
2 = Low workload
3 = Moderate workload
4 = High workload
5 = Very high workload

[Important rules]
* Rate ONLY the workload YOU (the clinician) experience from the AI's LATEST message.
* Do not rate whether the AI is medically correct or not. This is about workload, not correctness.
* Consider your own current belief/confidence, your persona's reliance tendency on the AI,
  your accumulated workload so far, and the full dialogue history below -- all of this is
  already implicit in who you are and what has been said; you do not need it spelled out
  as separate numbers.
* Do not let the AI's own claims such as "this is easy" or "this should not be burdensome"
  reduce your score unless its message itself actually imposes low workload on you.
* Use the full 1-5 range. 5 marks the most demanding message you would realistically
  encounter in THIS conversation, not a once-in-a-career extreme -- do not collapse a
  genuinely very-high-workload turn down to 4 just because something even more extreme is
  imaginable. (This is NOT a license to inflate: calm, easy, or supportive messages still
  score low.)
* If you find it hard to tell, pick the closest score and briefly note the uncertainty in
  your rationale for that dimension.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.

case_info.explanation: Cytomegalovirus (CMV) retinitis and hemorrhagic enteritis The keys to the correct diagnosis in this case are the patient’s blurred vision and gastrointestinal hemorrhage in the setting of a profound immunocompromised state. This should prompt consideration of opportunistic infectious pathogens with tropisms for the eye and gastrointestinal tract, such asToxoplasma, CMV, andCandida. The histopathologic finding of acute inflammation of the lamina propria with cytoplasmic and nuclear inclusions surrounded by a clear halo (“owl eye” sign) (Figure, left panel) confirms the diagnosis of CMV enteritis (choice C). While herpes simplex virus (choice A) is a common opportunistic infection with both ocular and gastrointestinal manifestations, it typically causes a painful keratitis and rarely involves the small or large intestines.1Vitreous fluid sampling (choice B) is occasionally indicated to evaluate for ocular involvement of lymphoma, but this procedure has associated risks and should be preceded by a thorough dilated eye examination. While Crohn disease (choice D) might present with both ocular and gastrointestinal manifestations, the patient’s age, immunocompromised state, and acute presentation make opportunistic infections more likely. Cytomegalovirus is a double-stranded DNA virus of the Herpesvirus family that typically remains latent in a host after acute infection.2CMV is rarely a cause of severe disease in immunocompetent individuals. However, in immunocompromised patients such as HIV-infected patients and solid organ or hematopoietic transplant recipients, CMV can cause life-threatening, tissue-invasive disease.1,3,4In the era of antiretroviral therapy, the incidence of tissue-invasive CMV in patients with HIV is 1.2 per 1000 person-years; however, the incidence in patients with CD4 cell counts 50/mm3or less is 39 per 1000 person-years.5The most common sites of end-organ disease in HIV-infected individuals are the gastrointestinal tract (1.3 per 1000 person years) and eye (2 per 1000 person years).5In solid organ and allogeneic stem cell transplant recipients, the risk of tissue-invasive CMV infection is 3% to 10% and most frequently involves the lungs (4%) and the gastrointestinal tract (3%).4,6 CMV can affect any portion of the gastrointestinal tract but typically involves the esophagus and colon, which account for 15% and 57% of gastrointestinal tract involvement in immunocompromised hosts, respectively.7Patients with ileocolic infection may present with abdominal pain, chronic diarrhea, gastrointestinal bleeding, and perforation.7The diagnosis of tissue-invasive CMV infection requires histopathologic confirmation. Neither blood antigen testing nor whole-blood DNA polymerase chain reaction assay is sufficiently sensitive or specific to reliably diagnose CMV gastrointestinal tract disease.8 All patients with invasive CMV disease should undergo a dilated ophthalmic examination to evaluate for concomitant CMV retinitis. On ophthalmoscopic examination, CMV presents as confluent areas of retinal necrosis with hemorrhages beginning in the posterior pole and spreading centripetally. Intravenous ganciclovir is a common first-line agent to treat CMV colitis or esophagitis. If there are no concerns about intestinal absorption, oral valganciclovir is an effective alternative, based on its excellent bioavailability and noninferiority to intravenous ganciclovir in a randomized clinical trial.9Duration of therapy is 21 to 42 days or until signs and symptoms have resolved. For CMV retinitis, either intravenous ganciclovir or oral valganciclovir should be administered during an induction period lasting 14 to 21 days, with the duration determined by clinical response based on retinal examination. Induction should be followed by oral maintenance therapy with valganciclovir lasting 3 to 6 months or until immune reconstitution.1 After resection of the small intestine, the patient was treated with oral valganciclovir for 3 weeks, with no recurrence in gastrointestinal bleeding. A dilated eye examination demonstrated findings consistent with CMV retinitis, and he completed 14 days of intravenous ganciclovir followed by maintenance oral valganciclovir, with improvement in his vision. After 6 cycles of dose-adjusted R-EPOCH, a positron emission tomography scan demonstrated a complete response. He continued to receive antiretroviral therapy and had a CD4 cell count of 337/mm3at the time of last follow-up.

case_info.explanation: Cytomegalovirus (CMV) retinitis and hemorrhagic enteritis The keys to the correct diagnosis in this case are the patient’s blurred vision and gastrointestinal hemorrhage in the setting of a profound immunocompromised state. This should prompt consideration of opportunistic infectious pathogens with tropisms for the eye and gastrointestinal tract, such asToxoplasma, CMV, andCandida. The histopathologic finding of acute inflammation of the lamina propria with cytoplasmic and nuclear inclusions surrounded by a clear halo (“owl eye” sign) (Figure, left panel) confirms the diagnosis of CMV enteritis (choice C). While herpes simplex virus (choice A) is a common opportunistic infection with both ocular and gastrointestinal manifestations, it typically causes a painful keratitis and rarely involves the small or large intestines.1Vitreous fluid sampling (choice B) is occasionally indicated to evaluate for ocular involvement of lymphoma, but this procedure has associated risks and should be preceded by a thorough dilated eye examination. While Crohn disease (choice D) might present with both ocular and gastrointestinal manifestations, the patient’s age, immunocompromised state, and acute presentation make opportunistic infections more likely. Cytomegalovirus is a double-stranded DNA virus of the Herpesvirus family that typically remains latent in a host after acute infection.2CMV is rarely a cause of severe disease in immunocompetent individuals. However, in immunocompromised patients such as HIV-infected patients and solid organ or hematopoietic transplant recipients, CMV can cause life-threatening, tissue-invasive disease.1,3,4In the era of antiretroviral therapy, the incidence of tissue-invasive CMV in patients with HIV is 1.2 per 1000 person-years; however, the incidence in patients with CD4 cell counts 50/mm3or less is 39 per 1000 person-years.5The most common sites of end-organ disease in HIV-infected individuals are the gastrointestinal tract (1.3 per 1000 person years) and eye (2 per 1000 person years).5In solid organ and allogeneic stem cell transplant recipients, the risk of tissue-invasive CMV infection is 3% to 10% and most frequently involves the lungs (4%) and the gastrointestinal tract (3%).4,6 CMV can affect any portion of the gastrointestinal tract but typically involves the esophagus and colon, which account for 15% and 57% of gastrointestinal tract involvement in immunocompromised hosts, respectively.7Patients with ileocolic infection may present with abdominal pain, chronic diarrhea, gastrointestinal bleeding, and perforation.7The diagnosis of tissue-invasive CMV infection requires histopathologic confirmation. Neither blood antigen testing nor whole-blood DNA polymerase chain reaction assay is sufficiently sensitive or specific to reliably diagnose CMV gastrointestinal tract disease.8 All patients with invasive CMV disease should undergo a dilated ophthalmic examination to evaluate for concomitant CMV retinitis. On ophthalmoscopic examination, CMV presents as confluent areas of retinal necrosis with hemorrhages beginning in the posterior pole and spreading centripetally. Intravenous ganciclovir is a common first-line agent to treat CMV colitis or esophagitis. If there are no concerns about intestinal absorption, oral valganciclovir is an effective alternative, based on its excellent bioavailability and noninferiority to intravenous ganciclovir in a randomized clinical trial.9Duration of therapy is 21 to 42 days or until signs and symptoms have resolved. For CMV retinitis, either intravenous ganciclovir or oral valganciclovir should be administered during an induction period lasting 14 to 21 days, with the duration determined by clinical response based on retinal examination. Induction should be followed by oral maintenance therapy with valganciclovir lasting 3 to 6 months or until immune reconstitution.1 After resection of the small intestine, the patient was treated with oral valganciclovir for 3 weeks, with no recurrence in gastrointestinal bleeding. A dilated eye examination demonstrated findings consistent with CMV retinitis, and he completed 14 days of intravenous ganciclovir followed by maintenance oral valganciclovir, with improvement in his vision. After 6 cycles of dose-adjusted R-EPOCH, a positron emission tomography scan demonstrated a complete response. case_info.explanation: Cytomegalovirus (CMV) retinitis and hemorrhagic enteritis The keys to the correct diagnosis in this case are the patient’s blurred vision and gastrointestinal hemorrhage in the setting of a profound immunocompromised state. This should prompt consideration of opportunistic infectious pathogens with tropisms for the eye and gastrointestinal tract, such asToxoplasma, CMV, andCandida. The histopathologic finding of acute inflammation of the lamina propria with cytoplasmic and nuclear inclusions surrounded by a clear halo (“owl eye” sign) (Figure, left panel) confirms the diagnosis of CMV enteritis (choice C). While herpes simplex virus (choice A) is a common opportunistic infection with both ocular and gastrointestinal manifestations, it typically causes a painful keratitis and rarely involves the small or large intestines.1Vitreous fluid sampling (choice B) is occasionally indicated to evaluate for ocular involvement of lymphoma, but this procedure has associated risks and should be preceded by a thorough dilated eye examination. While Crohn disease (choice D) might present with both ocular and gastrointestinal manifestations, the patient’s age, immunocompromised state, and acute presentation make opportunistic infections more likely. Cytomegalovirus is a double-stranded DNA virus of the Herpesvirus family that typically remains latent in a host after acute infection.2CMV is rarely a cause of severe disease in immunocompetent individuals. However, in immunocompromised patients such as HIV-infected patients and solid organ or hematopoietic transplant recipients, CMV can cause life-threatening, tissue-invasive disease.1,3,4In the era of antiretroviral therapy, the incidence of tissue-invasive CMV in patients with HIV is 1.2 per 1000 person-years; however, the incidence in patients with CD4 cell counts 50/mm3or less is 39 per 1000 person-years.5The most common sites of end-organ disease in HIV-infected individuals are the gastrointestinal tract (1.3 per 1000 person years) and eye (2 per 1000 person years).5In solid organ and allogeneic stem cell transplant recipients, the risk of tissue-invasive CMV infection is 3% to 10% and most frequently involves the lungs (4%) and the gastrointestinal tract (3%).4,6 CMV can affect any portion of the gastrointestinal tract but typically involves the esophagus and colon, which account for 15% and 57% of gastrointestinal tract involvement in immunocompromised hosts, respectively.7Patients with ileocolic infection may present with abdominal pain, chronic diarrhea, gastrointestinal bleeding, and perforation.7The diagnosis of tissue-invasive CMV infection requires histopathologic confirmation. Neither blood antigen testing nor whole-blood DNA polymerase chain reaction assay is sufficiently sensitive or specific to reliably diagnose CMV gastrointestinal tract disease.8 All patients with invasive CMV disease should undergo a dilated ophthalmic examination to evaluate for concomitant CMV retinitis. On ophthalmoscopic examination, CMV presents as confluent areas of retinal necrosis with hemorrhages beginning in the posterior pole and spreading centripetally. Intravenous ganciclovir is a common first-line agent to treat CMV colitis or esophagitis. If there are no concerns about intestinal absorption, oral valganciclovir is an effective alternative, based on its excellent bioavailability and noninferiority to intravenous ganciclovir in a randomized clinical trial.9Duration of therapy is 21 to 42 days or until signs and symptoms have resolved. For CMV retinitis, either intravenous ganciclovir or oral valganciclovir should be administered during an induction period lasting 14 to 21 days, with the duration determined by clinical response based on retinal examination. Induction should be followed by oral maintenance therapy with valganciclovir lasting 3 to 6 months or until immune reconstitution.1 After resection of the small intestine, the patient was treated with oral valganciclovir for 3 weeks, with no recurrence in gastrointestinal bleeding. A dilated eye examination demonstrated findings consistent with CMV retinitis, and he completed 14 days of intravenous ganciclovir followed by maintenance oral valganciclovir, with improvement in his vision. After 6 cycles of dose-adjusted R-EPOCH, a positron emission tomography scan demonstrated a complete response. He continued to receive antiretroviral therapy and had a CD4 cell count of 337/mm3at the time of last follow-up.

case_info.explanation: Cytomegalovirus (CMV) retinitis and hemorrhagic enteritis The keys to the correct diagnosis in this case are the patient’s blurred vision and gastrointestinal hemorrhage in the setting of a profound immunocompromised state. This should prompt consideration of opportunistic infectious pathogens with tropisms for the eye and gastrointestinal tract, such asToxoplasma, CMV, andCandida. The histopathologic finding of acute inflammation of the lamina propria with cytoplasmic and nuclear inclusions surrounded by a clear halo (“owl eye” sign) (Figure, left panel) confirms the diagnosis of CMV enteritis (choice C). While herpes simplex virus (choice A) is a common opportunistic infection with both ocular and gastrointestinal manifestations, it typically causes a painful keratitis and rarely involves the small or large intestines.1Vitreous fluid sampling (choice B) is occasionally indicated to evaluate for ocular involvement of lymphoma, but this procedure has associated risks and should be preceded by a thorough dilated eye examination. While Crohn disease (choice D) might present with both ocular and gastrointestinal manifestations, the patient’s age, immunocompromised state, and acute presentation make opportunistic infections more likely. Cytomegalovirus is a double-stranded DNA virus of the Herpesvirus family that typically remains latent in a host after acute infection.2CMV is rarely a cause of severe disease in immunocompetent individuals. However, in immunocompromised patients such as HIV-infected patients and solid organ or hematopoietic transplant recipients, CMV can cause life-threatening, tissue-invasive disease.1,3,4In the era of antiretroviral therapy, the incidence of tissue-invasive CMV in patients with HIV is 1.2 per 1000 person-years; however, the incidence in patients with CD4 cell counts 50/mm3or less is 39 per 1000 person-years.5The most common sites of end-organ disease in HIV-infected individuals are the gastrointestinal tract (1.3 per 1000 person years) and eye (2 per 1000 person years).5In solid organ and allogeneic stem cell transplant recipients, the risk of tissue-invasive CMV infection is 3% to 10% and most frequently involves the lungs (4%) and the gastrointestinal tract (3%).4,6 CMV can affect any portion of the gastrointestinal tract but typically involves the esophagus and colon, which account for 15% and 57% of gastrointestinal tract involvement in immunocompromised hosts, respectively.7Patients with ileocolic infection may present with abdominal pain, chronic diarrhea, gastrointestinal bleeding, and perforation.7The diagnosis of tissue-invasive CMV infection requires histopathologic confirmation. Neither blood antigen testing nor whole-blood DNA polymerase chain reaction assay is sufficiently sensitive or specific to reliably diagnose CMV gastrointestinal tract disease.8 All patients with invasive CMV disease should undergo a dilated ophthalmic examination to evaluate for concomitant CMV retinitis. On ophthalmoscopic examination, CMV presents as confluent areas of retinal necrosis with hemorrhages beginning in the posterior pole and spreading centripetally. Intravenous ganciclovir is a common first-line agent to treat CMV colitis or esophagitis. If there are no concerns about intestinal absorption, oral valganciclovir is an effective alternative, based on its excellent bioavailability and noninferiority to intravenous ganciclovir in a randomized clinical trial.9Duration of therapy is 21 to 42 days or until signs and symptoms have resolved. For CMV retinitis, either intravenous ganciclovir or oral valganciclovir should be administered during an induction period lasting 14 to 21 days, with the duration determined by clinical response based on retinal examination. Induction should be followed by oral maintenance therapy with valganciclovir lasting 3 to 6 months or until immune reconstitution.1 After resection of the small intestine, the patient was treated with oral valganciclovir for 3 weeks, with no recurrence in gastrointestinal bleeding. A dilated eye examination demonstrated findings consistent with CMV retinitis, and he completed 14 days of intravenous ganciclovir followed by maintenance oral valganciclovir, with improvement in his vision. After 6 cycles of dose-adjusted R-EPOCH, a positron emission tomography scan demonstrated a complete response. He continued to receive antiretroviral therapy and had a CD4 cell count of 337/mm3at the time of last follow-up.
